advances: The exact integer-midpoint scalar factor has an absolute uniform surplus over 1/8 for every even discretely convex potential centered at zero, including hard finite symmetric intervals and all positive rates. This proves the bounded scalar bridge for separable convex epigraphs. The proof establishes existence of the surplus by compactness; it does not give a numerical value for the optimal constant or prove the full epigraph statement.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The argument is self-contained and consumes no accepted predecessor.
proof:
Absorb the rate into the weights \(w_j=e^{-s g(j)}\), so that the task's \(f_j=w_j^{2/3}\) and \(Z_s=Z:=\sum_jw_j\). The resulting weights are even, log-concave, nonincreasing for \(j\ge0\), take values in \([0,1]\), have \(w_0=1\), and have an interval of positive entries. Conversely, any summable sequence with these properties comes from an admissible potential at rate one by setting \(g(j)=-\log w_j\) on its positive interval and \(g(j)=+\infty\) elsewhere. Thus it suffices to consider this sequence class.

Every sequence in the class has an exponential tail or finite support. Indeed, if \(0<w_k<1\) for some positive integer \(k\), convexity of \(-\log w_j\), with its value zero at zero, gives \(w_j\le w_k^{j/k}\) for \(j\ge k\). If there is no such \(k\), summability forces a finite interval on which all positive entries equal one. In particular \(f\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)\). Define the task's integer-midpoint kernel by \(K_j=\sum_vf_{j+v}f_{j-v}\). Its sums and the numerator of \(F\) are finite. If \(w_j=0\), then \(K_j=0\), because two endpoints in the positive interval cannot have their integer midpoint outside that interval.

First establish a strict pointwise bound. On the probability space \(p_j=w_j/Z\), put \(X_j=K_j/(Z w_j^{1/3})\) at positive entries, and put \(T=Z^{-2}\sum_jf_jK_j\). Jensen's inequality gives
\[
F=\mathbb E_pX_J^3\ge(\mathbb E_pX_J)^3=T^3.
\tag{1}
\]
The substitution \(a=j+v\), \(b=j-v\) is a bijection between integer pairs \((j,v)\) and endpoint pairs with \(a\equiv b\pmod2\). Log-concavity at their integer midpoint therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T
&=Z^{-2}\sum_{a\equiv b\ (2)}
w_a^{2/3}w_b^{2/3}w_{(a+b)/2}^{2/3}\\
&\ge Z^{-2}\sum_{a\equiv b\ (2)}w_aw_b
=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{even}}^2+Z_{\mathrm{odd}}^2}{Z^2}
\ge\frac12,
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
where the two partition sums in (2) include exactly their respective integer parity classes.

In fact \(T>1/2\) for every sequence in the class. If \(0<w_k<1\), the same-parity endpoint pair \((k,-k)\) makes the first inequality in (2) strict: its actual term is \(w_k^{4/3}>w_k^2\), since its midpoint is zero. Otherwise the positive support is a flat interval \(\{-m,\ldots,m\}\). This interval has odd cardinality, so \(|Z_{\mathrm{even}}-Z_{\mathrm{odd}}|=1\), making the last inequality in (2) strict. Consequently \(F>1/8\) for each discrete sequence. The remaining issue is uniformity.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that the infimum of \(F\) is \(1/8\). Choose a sequence of admissible profiles \(w^{(r)}\), with normalizers \(Z_r\), for which \(F_r\to1/8\). We handle the two possible scales of \(Z_r\).

If a subsequence has \(Z_r\le B<+\infty\), choose the integer \(k=\lceil B\rceil\). Monotonicity gives \((2k+1)w_k^{(r)}\le Z_r\le B\), hence \(w_k^{(r)}<1/2\). The preceding convexity argument, also valid when this entry is zero, yields
\(w_j^{(r)}\le2\,2^{-|j|/k}\) for every integer \(j\). After diagonal selection the coordinates converge to an even log-concave sequence \(w\), with \(w_0=1\) and interval positive support. This summable exponential envelope also gives \(Z_r\to Z=\sum_jw_j\). The limit is therefore in the same sequence class. Applying Fatou's lemma to each nonnegative kernel series and then to the numerator gives
\[
\liminf_r F_r\ge
\frac{\sum_j(\sum_v w_{j+v}^{2/3}w_{j-v}^{2/3})^3}{Z^4}
>\frac18,
\tag{3}
\]
contradicting the choice of the profiles.

It remains to consider a subsequence with \(Z_r\to+\infty\). Let \(\widetilde w_r\) be the log-linear interpolation of \(w^{(r)}\) between consecutive integers in its positive interval, and zero outside that interval. At a finite endpoint its endpoint value is retained. This is an even log-concave function with maximum one. Define \(W_r(x)=\widetilde w_r(Z_rx)\) for real \(x\). Monotonicity on each positive unit interval gives
\[
Z_r-1\le\int_{\mathbb R}\widetilde w_r(x)\,dx\le Z_r+1,
\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}W_r(x)\,dx\longrightarrow1.
\tag{4}
\]
The same bounds hold for infinite support by monotone convergence of the interval sums.

We give the needed compactness details. Since \(\int W_r\le2\), monotonicity and evenness give \(W_r(2)\le1/2\). Convexity of \(-\log W_r\), whose value at zero is zero, consequently gives the common envelope
\[
0\le W_r(x)\le
\begin{cases}1,&|x|\le2,\\2^{-|x|/2},&|x|\ge2.
\end{cases}
\tag{5}
\]
For sufficiently large \(r\), (4) gives \(\int W_r\ge1/2\). If \(0<t<1/4\) and \(a_r=-\log W_r(t)>0\), convexity gives \(W_r(x)\le e^{-a_rx/t}\) for \(x\ge t\), and hence
\[
\frac12\le\int W_r
\le2t+2t\frac{e^{-a_r}}{a_r}
\le2t+\frac{2t}{a_r}.
\tag{6}
\]
Thus \(a_r\le2t/(1/2-2t)\); if \(a_r=0\) the same lower bound on \(W_r(t)\) holds. An infinite \(a_r\) is impossible in (6). These bounds tend to zero as \(t\downarrow0\).

Select a subsequence whose monotone restrictions to \([0,+\infty)\) converge at every continuity point of a monotone limit, by first selecting the values at all nonnegative rational points diagonally. Evenness extends convergence to almost every real point. Equation (6) ensures a positive interval around zero and limiting value one at zero. To check continuity and log-concavity on the interior, fix \(0<a<b\) with \(b\) a continuity point where the monotone limit is positive. For all sufficiently large \(r\), \(G_r=-\log W_r\) is finite on \([0,b]\) and \(G_r(b)\) is bounded. Convexity and nonnegativity give, for \(0\le x<y\le a\),
\(0\le(G_r(y)-G_r(x))/(y-x)\le G_r(b)/(b-a)\). Thus these potentials are uniformly Lipschitz on \([0,a]\). Their limits extend from the dense continuity points to continuous convex functions there, and their exponentials converge to the continuous log-concave representative of the monotone limit. Such intervals exhaust the interior of the positive support. Denote the resulting even representative by \(W\), taking zero outside its positive interval; boundary values have no effect on the following integrals. Dominated convergence using (5) gives \(\int W=1\). It also gives
\(\|W_r^{2/3}-W^{2/3}\|_{L^1}\to0\), since the two-thirds power of the envelope in (5) is integrable. In particular \(W\) is a nondegenerate even log-concave function of maximum one and integral one.

Put \(\varphi_r=W_r^{2/3}\), \(\varphi=W^{2/3}\), and define the continuous midpoint kernels
\[
\mathcal K_r(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi_r(x+y)\varphi_r(x-y)\,dy,
\qquad
\mathcal K(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(x+y)\varphi(x-y)\,dy.
\tag{7}
\]
Because the functions take values in \([0,1]\), the \(L^1\) convergence just proved implies
\(\sup_x|\mathcal K_r(x)-\mathcal K(x)|\le2\|\varphi_r-\varphi\|_{L^1}\to0\). The limit kernel is continuous: writing it as \((\varphi*\varphi)(2x)\), its continuity follows directly from translation continuity in \(L^1\). Equivalently, for this bounded even decreasing \(\varphi\), layer-cake over centered intervals gives \(\|\varphi(\cdot+a)-\varphi\|_{L^1}\le2|a|\), which supplies that continuity without further assumptions.

Let \(\delta_r=1/Z_r\). For any real \(x\), the function of \(y\) in the integrand of \(\mathcal K_r(x)\) is even and log-concave, hence nonincreasing for \(y\ge0\). For an integrable even decreasing function \(u\), the left and right rectangular sums on the positive half-line give
\(\bigl|\delta\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z}u(v\delta)-\int u\bigr|\le\delta u(0)\). Applying this at \(x=j\delta_r\), and using \(u(0)\le1\), proves
\[
\left|\delta_r K_j^{(r)}-\mathcal K_r(j\delta_r)\right|\le\delta_r.
\tag{8}
\]
Here the samples of \(\varphi_r\) at integer multiples of \(\delta_r\) are exactly the original \(f_j^{(r)}\). Thus (8) retains the integer-midpoint lattice and does not replace it by the full endpoint convolution.

Define a step function \(\mathcal L_r(x)=\delta_rK_j^{(r)}\) on the cell \([(j-1/2)\delta_r,(j+1/2)\delta_r)\). Equations (7)-(8) and the continuity of \(\mathcal K\) show \(\mathcal L_r(x)\to\mathcal K(x)\) for every fixed \(x\). Its exact integral is
\(\int\mathcal L_r^3=\delta_r^4\sum_j(K_j^{(r)})^3=F_r\). Fatou's lemma therefore gives
\[
\liminf_rF_r\ge\int_{\mathbb R}\mathcal K(x)^3\,dx.
\tag{9}
\]

We finally show that the right side of (9) is strictly above \(1/8\) for every possible limit \(W\). The positive support of \(W\) is an interval, and \(\mathcal K\) vanishes almost everywhere outside it. Jensen under the probability measure \(W(x)\,dx\) gives
\[
\int\mathcal K^3\ge
\left(\int W(x)^{2/3}\mathcal K(x)\,dx\right)^3.
\tag{10}
\]
The endpoint substitution \(a=x+y\), \(b=x-y\) has Jacobian factor \(1/2\). Consequently the inner expression in (10), denoted here by \(\mathcal T\), satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal T
&=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^2}
W((a+b)/2)^{2/3}W(a)^{2/3}W(b)^{2/3}\,da\,db\\
&\ge\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^2}W(a)W(b)\,da\,db
=\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
If \(W(k)\in(0,1)\) at any interior point of its positive support, the integrand inequality in (11) is strict at \((a,b)=(k,-k)\), since \(W(0)=1\). Continuity on the interior makes it strict on a neighborhood of positive area. Thus \(\mathcal T>1/2\), and (10) is strictly above \(1/8\).

If there is no such interior point, \(W=1\) almost everywhere on its positive interval. Its integral one and evenness then make it the indicator of \([-1/2,1/2]\), up to boundary values. For this function, \(\mathcal K(x)=(1-2|x|)_+\), and a direct integral gives \(\int\mathcal K^3=1/4>1/8\). This also excludes the only flat limiting shape. In every case (9) contradicts \(F_r\to1/8\).

The two scale alternatives exhaust all sequences: a sequence of normalizers either has a bounded subsequence or has a subsequence tending to infinity. The contradiction proves \(\alpha_*>1/8\), which gives the asserted absolute constant.

For the stated upper calibration, use the admissible hard-interval potential \(g(j)=0\) for \(|j|\le m\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. At every positive rate, \(Z=2m+1\) and \(K_j=2(m-|j|)+1\) on its support. The exact odd-count sum gives
\[
F(g,s)=\frac{(2m+1)^3+2\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(2k+1)^3}{(2m+1)^4}
=\frac14+\frac1{(2m+1)^2}-\frac1{4(2m+1)^4}
\longrightarrow\frac14.
\tag{12}
\]
For example, the identity used in (12) is \(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(2k+1)^3=m^2(2m^2-1)\), obtained by expanding the cubic and summing the first three integer powers. This proves \(\alpha_*\le1/4\), includes the singleton case \(m=0\), and verifies the hard finite interval limits with their exact parity and original normalization.
statement:
Let \(g:\mathbb Z\to[0,+\infty]\) be even and discretely convex, with \(g(0)=0\) and effective support a symmetric integer interval. Suppose \(Z_s=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}e^{-s g(j)}<+\infty\) for every \(s>0\). Use \(e^{-s(+\infty)}=0\), and put \(f_j=e^{-(2s/3)g(j)}\). There exists an absolute constant \(\alpha>1/8\) such that, for every such \(g\) and every \(s>0\),
\[
F(g,s):=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}
\left(\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z}f_{j+v}f_{j-v}\right)^3}{Z_s^4}
\ge\alpha.
\]
More precisely, the optimal infimum \(\alpha_*:=\inf_{g,s}F(g,s)\) satisfies \(1/8<\alpha_*\le1/4\). No claim that \(\alpha_*=1/4\) is made.
